Ibn 'Ashur holds that the charity was prescribed for the benefit of the poor and to honour the Prophet, that it was practised only briefly, and that scholars agree it was abrogated. Al-Shawkani reads the command as a recommendation, and holds that one who forgoes private conversation with the Prophet does not fall short. All agree that a poor believer who cannot give is excused.

This verse tells believers who wish to speak privately with the Prophet ﷺ to give charity beforehand. It then says that God has relieved them of this duty after it proved hard for them: the question means, as most commentators read it, "Were you afraid of poverty by giving charity before your private talks?" Since you did not do so and God has pardoned you, keep up the prayer, pay the zakat, and obey God and His Messenger; God is fully aware of what you do. The commentators broadly agree that the charity was meant to help the poor and to reduce the constant demands on the Prophet ﷺ, and that the previous verse is its cause. The disagreement centres on abrogation. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the ruling was abrogated, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy reporting that Ali ibn Abi Talib alone acted on it. Muqatil ibn Hayyan speaks of ten nights, while al-Kalbi and Qatada speak of a single hour of the day. Ibn 'Atiyya rejects the abrogation as unsupported and considers the command a recommendation, a view shared by al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur. Al-Qasimi records Abu Muslim's position that the duty was time-limited and not abrogated at all.

God addresses His Prophet ﷺ in wonder about the hypocrites who took as allies a people upon whom God is angry, namely the Jews, advising them and passing on the secrets of the believers. According to most commentators, the phrase 'they are neither of you nor of them' means that the hypocrites were truly neither believers nor Jews, but wavered between the two camps, as the verse 'wavering between that and this' also says. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand the false oath as their claim to be Muslims. The clause 'while they know' indicates, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, that the lie was deliberate. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan propose a different reading of the pronouns, so that 'they are not of you' refers to the Jews and 'nor of them' to the hypocrites, which would make their alliance even more reprehensible since they belong to neither side. Ibn 'Ashur also allows that the hypocrites' Islam was not sincere. On the occasion of revelation, most commentators, including al-Suyuti, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, mention Abd Allah ibn Nabtal, who mocked the Prophet and then swore he had not done so. Al-Tabari also relates a hadith about a man with blue eyes. Some, such as al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi, extend the meaning to the Day of Resurrection, when the hypocrites will swear to God as they once swore to the believers. Al-Razi uses the verse to refute al-Jahiz's definition of a lie.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns the hypocrites who allied themselves with the Jews and passed on the secrets of the believers, and that God has prepared for them a severe punishment because of their repeated evil deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand the severe punishment as the punishment of the Hereafter, while al-Razi reports that some scholars take it to mean the punishment of the grave. As for the phrase "evil were their deeds," Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain it as habitual practice and prolonged persistence in wrongdoing, and al-Zamakhshari sees in it an emphasis on their past obstinacy.

The commentators agree that the hypocrites falsely swore to the believers that they were of them, and that their oaths served as a shield against death and harm. Through these oaths they "barred from the way of God", which according to the views means turning others away from Islam, or turning the believers away from fighting them. Al-Tabari notes that God's ruling regarding disbelieving People of the Book is killing or the poll tax, and that the hypocrites thus prevented their being killed. Al-Qurtubi reports that al-Hasan's reading "iman" with a kasra means the profession of faith they adopted out of fear of death, while their hearts remained disbelieving. The humiliating punishment is for them in the Hereafter.

Opinions differ on the meaning of "fa-sadduu": Ibn 'Atiyya allows that the verb may be intransitive or transitive, while al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari take it to mean turning others away from Islam or the believers away from fighting them. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that these oaths were sworn in worldly life. The commentators present these different positions without judging between them.

This verse describes hypocrites who used their oaths as a shield: through false swearing they protected themselves and their property, and by this they turned people away from the way of God, so they deserve a humiliating punishment. The commentators agree that these men swore to the believers that they belonged to them when they did not, and that junna means a cover or shelter one hides behind. Al-Tabari explains that the ruling for disbelievers among the People of the Book was killing or the poll tax, and for idolaters killing; the hypocrites prevented the believers from killing them by swearing to their faith. Ibn Kathir says they displayed belief while concealing disbelief, so that many who did not know their true state were deceived, which amounted to a turning away from the path. Ibn al-Jawzi, quoting Ibn Qutayba, reports that they swore whenever something threatened to bring them punishment.

The meaning of the turning away is disputed. Al-Sudi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean turning people away from Islam; al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take it to mean hindering believers from fighting or killing them. Al-Hasan read "imanahum" with a kasra, giving the sense that their profession of faith served as the shield, as reported by al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan. As for the humiliating punishment, al-Tabari applies it to Hell, while al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud understand it as punishment in the afterlife; some note that the severe punishment mentioned just before may refer to the punishment of the grave, which would avoid repetition in their view.

This verse states that neither their wealth nor their children will shield the hypocrites from God's punishment, and that they are the companions of the Fire, where they will abide forever. The commentators identify these people as the hypocrites who sided with the Jews and passed on the secrets of the believers; the phrase "neither of you nor of them" describes them as wavering between the two groups. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that their oath on the Day of Resurrection will be like the oaths they swore in this world, whereas al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi hold that the people of the Hereafter do not lie, so their oath would mean that they were not disbelievers inwardly. Al-Razi rejects this reading as weakening the coherence of the text.

The commentators agree that their false oaths served as a shield against being killed, and that they used them to turn others away from God's path. The meaning of "turning away from God's path" is disputed: al-Suddi takes it as keeping people from Islam, while Muqatil, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir understand it as obstructing the struggle in jihad. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the wonder lies in their lying before the One who knows the unseen. Ibn 'Ashur links the passage to their pride in their wealth and tribes, which the verse sets aside.

The phrases "humiliating punishment" and "the fire" are read by al-Razi as two stages, one in the grave and one in the Hereafter, an opinion that others do not share.

The plain meaning of the verse is that on the Day God raises all of them, the hypocrites will swear to Him as they swore to the believers in this life, thinking their oaths will benefit them, and God declares that they are the liars. The commentators agree that the verse speaks of the hypocrites and portrays their persistence in falsehood. Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi explain that being on something means being on something beneficial, while the Jalalayn, Ibn Sa'di and others say they expect their oaths to profit them before God as they did before people. Ibn Kathir understands that they believe they are upon guidance, since a person dies and is raised upon what he lived by. Ibn 'Ashur cites the hadith that each servant is raised upon what he died upon, to show that hypocrisy remains in them after resurrection. Qurtubi and al-Nasafi see this as self-deception, and Abu Hayyan marvels that they think their disbelief can be hidden from the Knower of the unseen. Opinions differ on the oath itself. Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur hold that it is a genuine lie in the Hereafter. Al-Razi reports that al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi held that people of the Hereafter do not lie, so the oath would mean that they did not consider themselves unbelievers inwardly, a reading he finds weakens the wording of the text. Qurtubi says the more apparent view is that this delusion concerns the Hereafter, while noting another view that places it in this world.

This verse describes those whom Satan has come to dominate, so that they forget the remembrance of God; they are Satan's party, and they are the losers. Al-Tabari reads istahwadha as overpowering them, while al-Mawardi, citing al-Mufaddal, gives the sense of encircling them, and al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi add that this domination lasts in this world. Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan link the verb to the image of a driver gathering and herding a flock, so that Satan has gathered them as his followers. As for forgetting God's remembrance, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan say it may mean heedlessness or abandoning obedience, and Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Sa'di stress that they no longer remember God either in heart or tongue. Al-Nasafi, quoting Shah al-Kirmani, describes the sign of this domination as a man absorbed in his appetites and worldly concerns. All commentators understand hizb as Satan's troops or followers. On their loss, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur explain it as losing God's pleasure and Paradise. They all connect the verse to the context of the hypocrites who allied themselves with the Jews and swore false oaths, though its wording is general and applies to anyone who takes this path.

This verse states that those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, transgressing their limits and commands, are among the most humiliated of creatures. The commentators explain that the word muhadda means hostility and opposition, and that whoever stands outside the limits set by God takes the position of an enemy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the humiliation of these people follows from the victory of God and His messengers, since the defeat of one party is proportional to the might of the other. Al-Razi adds that since God's might is infinite, the humiliation of those who oppose Him is also without limit.

The next verse, 'God has decreed: I and My messengers shall surely prevail,' is read by all as a promise of victory. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy understand it as a fixed and unchangeable decree. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress the superlative sense of 'among the most humiliated.' Al-Zajjaj, quoted by al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, distinguishes two ways in which the messengers prevail: by war for those sent with that mission, and by argument for those who were not commanded to fight.

The commentators relate these verses to episodes from the Prophet's life. Several cases are mentioned, including Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, who killed his father at Badr, and the accounts concerning Abu Bakr, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and 'Ali. Ibn Kathir also cites other reports. These traditions are not unanimous, and the commentators do not decide between them. All agree, however, on the general meaning: the believer must not befriend those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they are close relatives.

The commentators explain that this verse means God has decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet that He and His messengers will prevail over their opponents. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that God has ruled that victory belongs to Him, to His messengers and to His believing servants, in this world and the next. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi hold that the messengers prevail by proof for all, and by the sword for those who were commanded to fight, a distinction also made by al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the messengers differed: some combined argument with warfare, others relied on argument alone. The verse follows the statement that those who oppose God and His messenger are among the humiliated, which Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan connect to that humiliation. Readers differ on the vowel of the word 'wa-rusuli': Nafi' and Ibn Amir read it with a fatha. According to Muqatil, it was revealed after believers hoped to defeat Persia and Byzantium, and Abd Allah ibn Ubayy dissuaded them by praising the might of those empires. Al-Shinqiti argues that a prophet killed in battle does not contradict the promise, since the slain is not a victor. Al-Sha'rawi sees the verse as strengthening believers' confidence in divine help. Ibn Sa'di and the Tafsir al-Muyassar affirm that victory and the good end belong to the believers.

This verse states that you will not find true believers in God and the Last Day who show affection toward those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they are their own fathers, sons, brothers or clan. The commentators agree that faith and such loyalty cannot coexist in one heart. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain the phrase as referring to those who oppose God and His Messenger, while al-Mawardi gives three senses: fighting, disobeying or being hostile. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi explain that mawadda is a mutual affection, and al-Razi notes that some hold that such love and faith never meet in the heart while others see it as a grave sin that does not expel a person from Islam. The occasions of revelation vary: Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah killing his father, Abu Bakr confronting his son, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his brother, or Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a writing to the Meccans. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur treat these reports as examples of the ruling rather than its only cause, and Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the condemnation of the hypocrites. Malik derived from it the duty to shun the Qadariyya, while al-Thawri applied it to those who keep company with rulers. The verse closes by saying that God has written faith in their hearts, strengthened them with a spirit from Him, will admit them to gardens where they abide forever, that God is pleased with them and they with Him, and that they are the party of God, the successful ones.
